Table 5 on page 8 shows the maximum distance between municipal and C/Z-T/A boundaries for 18 cities as related to existing and proposed population—mileage formulas. Although measurements are approximate, they indicate that 13 of the 18 cities have C/Z's-T/A's which would fall within boundaries that would result from applying the proposed population-mileage formula.
Considered pertinent also to measurement of sprawl are the distances from municipal limits to the most distant commercial/industrial locations considered to be within the outlying developments of the municipalities. Table 6 records these distances as obtained from land use maps, and information from municipal/county/regional planners. Table 6, beginning on page 9, represents a sample of 34 cities which were selected on the basis of information being available from land use maps or city/county/regional planners. Efforts were directed toward obtaining a sample of cities in each population size groups which appear in the proposed population-mileage formula. The 34 city sample includes 14 for which C/Z's-T/A's are specifically defined by the Commission.
An analysis of Table 6 appears in Table 7 on page 10. The results indicate that for municipalities up to 25,000 in population there is a need for the proposed formula for 2 out of 14 places in the sample but that the existing formula embraces the most distant commercial/industrial locations in most instances.
For populations above 25,000 persons, it appears that both the existing and the proposed population-mileage formulas become progressively less adequate insofar as encompassing the most distant commercial/industrial locations within the geography determined by application of the formulas. The sample represented in Tables 6 and 7 is relatively small and is not presented as being representative of all U.S. municipalities. However, analysis of that sample does reveal the additional fact that the extent of decentralization and sprawl of commerce and industry varies widely for cities in the same population group, particularly for cities of 500,000 population or more. The patterns of spatial growth and development are not highly uniform among cities.
